## Current Projects

### Quantifying the Economic Cost of Pollution: The Impact of Air Pollution on Mental Health in England {#pollution-mental-health .paper-title}

revise and resubmit, *Journal of Environmental Economics and Management*

[Paper (PDF)](paper1.pdf)

**Abstract:** Air pollution poses significant health risks, with its impact on physical health well documented. However, there is limited causal evidence focusing on mental health. I estimate the mental health costs attributable to air pollution, using administrative data on monthly general practice-level medicine prescriptions from all public general practices in England between 2014 and 2019. Using an instrumental variable method, I exploit exogenous variations in air pollution driven by wind direction. I find that air pollution causally increases prescribing for two out of four categories of mental health conditions: 1) depression and chronic anxiety, and 2) psychoses and related disorders, but no effects on ADHD or insomnia and acute anxiety. A sustained 1 µg/m³ increase in fine particulate matter (with a standard deviation of 2.9 µg/m³) causes an additional £14.99 million in annual primary care psychiatric medication expenditure in England. Decomposing the effect with supplementary annual data suggests that pollution triggers new depression episodes and delays recovery, while the psychoses effect may reflect increased treatment intensity rather than new diagnoses. Heterogeneity analyses suggest that the mental health burden of air pollution falls disproportionately on vulnerable people, exacerbating existing health inequalities.

### Air Pollution, Labour Supply and Mental Health over the Life Cycle {#life-cycle .paper-title}

work in progress

**Abstract:** Mental health is influenced by both environmental conditions and labour market experiences, yet little is known about how these effects interact over the life cycle. I study this interaction by combining data from the UK Household Longitudinal Study with high-resolution measures of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) and weather conditions. I develop and estimate a dynamic model in which latent mental health, inferred from multiple survey measures, evolves jointly with labour market status. Identification exploits short-run variation in pollution exposure driven by wind direction and long-run variation from a shift-share design combining local emission source composition with national sector-specific changes in emissions. The model separates transitory from persistent effects of pollution, distinguishes direct effects from those operating through the labour market, and allows these effects to vary with age. I use the model to quantify the long-run mental health consequences of pollution exposure and to examine the potential complementarity between labour market interventions and pollution reduction in improving mental health.
